## What is pandas?

::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="50%"}
- The standard Python library for **tabular data**: rows and columns, like a spreadsheet or an R `data.frame`.
- Built on NumPy arrays, so it is fast for numeric work.
- Reads and writes CSV, Excel, JSON, parquet, SQL...
- Plots via matplotlib, and integrates with seaborn, scikit-learn, statsmodels...

```python
import pandas as pd
```
:::
::: {.column width="50%"}
Two objects do almost all the work:

| Object | Shape | R analogue |
|---|---|---|
| `Series` | 1-D, labelled | named vector |
| `DataFrame` | 2-D table | `data.frame` / tibble |

A `DataFrame` is a **dict of Series** that share the same row index.
:::
:::

## Series and DataFrame

::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="50%"}
```{python}
weights = pd.Series(
    [68, 83, 112],
    index=["alice", "bob", "charles"],
    name="weight")
weights
```
:::
::: {.column width="50%"}
```{python}
people = pd.DataFrame({
    "weight": [68, 83, 112],
    "height": [172, 181, 185],
    "hobby":  ["Biking", "Dancing", None],
}, index=["alice", "bob", "charles"])
people
```
:::
:::

Every column of a `DataFrame` is a `Series`, and every `Series` prints its `dtype` (and `Name`) at the bottom.

## The index: labels vs positions

Every pandas object carries an **index** of row labels. You can select by *label* or by *position*, and it pays to be explicit.

::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="50%"}
```{python}
weights.loc["bob"]     # by label
```
```{python}
weights.iloc[1]        # by position (0-based!)
```
:::
::: {.column width="50%"}
```{python}
weights.loc["alice":"bob"]   # label slices are inclusive
```
```{python}
weights.iloc[0:2]            # position slices are not
```
:::
:::

# Section 1: Series and DataFrames

## Creating a Series

::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="50%"}
From a list (default integer index):

```{python}
pd.Series([68, 83, 112])
```
:::
::: {.column width="50%"}
From a dict (keys become labels):

```{python}
heights = pd.Series({"alice": 172, "bob": 181,
                     "charles": 185, "darwin": 178},
                    name="height")
heights
```
:::
:::

## Selecting and filtering in Series

::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="50%"}
```{python}
weights[["bob", "charles"]]
```
```{python}
weights.iloc[[0, 2]]
```
:::
::: {.column width="50%"}
A condition gives a boolean Series, which filters:

```{python}
weights > 70
```
```{python}
weights[weights > 70]
```
:::
:::

## Operations on Series

::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="50%"}
Elementwise maths and **broadcasting** of scalars:

```{python}
weights + 5
```
```{python}
np.log(weights)
```
:::
::: {.column width="50%"}
Two Series are **aligned on their index** first. Labels present on one side only become `NaN`:

```{python}
weights / (heights / 100) ** 2
```
:::
:::

## Plotting a Series

```{python}
#| fig-align: center
weights.plot(kind="bar", title="Weight (kg)", figsize=(6, 3.2))
plt.show()
```

## Creating a DataFrame

::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="50%"}
From a dict of lists:

```{python}
pd.DataFrame({
    "weight":    [68, 83, 112],
    "birthyear": [1985, 1984, 1992],
}, index=["alice", "bob", "charles"])
```
:::
::: {.column width="50%"}
From a dict of Series &mdash; aligned on their index, gaps become `NaN`:

```{python}
pd.DataFrame({
    "weight":   pd.Series([68, 83], index=["alice", "bob"]),
    "children": pd.Series([3, 0], index=["bob", "charles"]),
})
```
:::
:::

## Selecting and filtering in DataFrames

::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="50%"}
```{python}
people["hobby"]              # one column -> Series
```
```{python}
people.loc["bob"]            # one row -> Series
```
:::
::: {.column width="50%"}
```{python}
people.loc["bob", "hobby"]   # row and column
```
```{python}
people[people["weight"] > 70]   # boolean mask
```
:::
:::

## Transposing and methods

::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="50%"}
```{python}
people.T
```
:::
::: {.column width="50%"}
Functions live *on* the object: `df.mean()`, not `mean(df)`.

```{python}
people.mean(numeric_only=True)
```
```{python}
people["hobby"].value_counts()
```
:::
:::

## Adding, removing and assigning columns

::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="50%"}
Treat it like a dict:

```{python}
people["age"] = 2026 - pd.Series([1985, 1984, 1992],
                                 index=people.index)
del people["hobby"]
people
```
:::
::: {.column width="50%"}
`assign()` returns a **new** DataFrame; a `lambda` sees the intermediate result, so calls chain:

```{python}
(people
   .assign(bmi=lambda df: df["weight"] / (df["height"] / 100) ** 2)
   .assign(overweight=lambda df: df["bmi"] > 25))
```
:::
:::

::: {.callout-warning}
`new = people` does **not** copy. Use `people.copy()`.
:::

# Section 2: Working with real data

## Loading data from CSV

```{python}
col_names = ["ID", "Diagnosis"] + [
    f"{m}{i}" for i in (1, 2, 3)
    for m in ("radius", "texture", "perimeter", "area", "smoothness", "compactness",
              "concavity", "concave_points", "symmetry", "fractal_dimension")]

wdbc = pd.read_csv("../workshop/data/wdbc.data.csv", header=None, names=col_names)
wdbc.head()
```

The file has no header row, so we pass `header=None` and supply `names=`. `read_csv` also accepts URLs.

## Handling missing data

::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="50%"}
```{python}
wdbc.isnull().sum().sort_values(ascending=False).head(4)
```
```{python}
clean = wdbc.dropna().drop_duplicates()
wdbc.shape, clean.shape
```
:::
::: {.column width="50%"}
Fill instead of drop, one column at a time:

```{python}
wdbc["texture1"] = wdbc["texture1"].fillna(wdbc["texture1"].mean())
wdbc["texture1"].isnull().sum()
```

Assign back with `=`. The chained `df[col].fillna(x, inplace=True)` pattern is deprecated.
:::
:::

## Overview functions

::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="50%"}
```{python}
clean.shape
```
```{python}
clean["Diagnosis"].value_counts()
```
```{python}
clean.dtypes.head(4)
```
:::
::: {.column width="50%"}
```{python}
clean[["radius1", "texture1", "area1"]].describe()
```
:::
:::

Also: `head()`, `tail()`, `info()`.

## Aggregating with groupby

Split by the values of a column, apply a summary to each group, combine the results.

::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="50%"}
```{python}
clean.groupby("Diagnosis")["radius1"].mean()
```
:::
::: {.column width="50%"}
```{python}
clean.groupby("Diagnosis")[["radius1", "area1"]].agg(["mean", "std"])
```
:::
:::

## Saving to files

```{python}
#| eval: false
clean.to_csv("data/cleaned_wdbc.csv", index=False)
clean.to_excel("data/cleaned_wdbc.xlsx", index=False)
clean.to_parquet("data/cleaned_wdbc.parquet")
```

Every reader has a matching writer: `read_csv` / `to_csv`, `read_excel` / `to_excel`, `read_json` / `to_json`, `read_parquet` / `to_parquet`, `read_sql` / `to_sql`.

## Plotting data

```{python}
#| fig-align: center
colours = clean["Diagnosis"].map({"B": "tab:blue", "M": "tab:red"})
clean.plot(kind="scatter", x="radius1", y="texture1", c=colours, alpha=0.5, figsize=(6, 2.6))
plt.show()
```

For richer statistical graphics use **seaborn**, which understands DataFrames directly (see the notebook).

# Section 3: Advanced DataFrame operations

```{python}
#| echo: false
people = pd.DataFrame({
    "weight":  [68, 83, 112],
    "height":  [172, 181, 185],
    "hobby":   ["Biking", "Dancing", np.nan],
    "age":     [41, 42, 34],
    "pets":    [np.nan, 0.0, 5.0],
}, index=["alice", "bob", "charles"])
```

## Evaluating an expression and querying

Write the formula as a string; refer to columns by name; `@` reaches Python variables.

::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="50%"}
```{python}
people.eval("bmi = weight / (height / 100) ** 2", inplace=True)
people
```
:::
::: {.column width="50%"}
```{python}
threshold = 30
people.query("age > 40 and bmi < @threshold")
```
:::
:::

::: {.callout-note}
On Google Colab add `engine="python"` to `eval` and `query` calls.
:::

## Sorting a DataFrame

::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="50%"}
```{python}
people.sort_index(ascending=False)
```
:::
::: {.column width="50%"}
```{python}
people.sort_values(by="age")
```
:::
:::

Both return a sorted copy; pass `inplace=True` to modify in place. `sort_index(axis=1)` sorts the columns.

## Operations on DataFrames

```{python}
scores = pd.DataFrame([[8, 8, 9], [10, 9, 9], [4, 8, 2], [9, 10, 10]],
                      columns=["sep", "oct", "nov"],
                      index=["alice", "bob", "charles", "darwin"])
```

::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="33%"}
```{python}
scores + 1
```
:::
::: {.column width="33%"}
```{python}
(scores > 5).all(axis=1)
```
:::
::: {.column width="33%"}
```{python}
scores - scores.mean()
```
:::
:::

## Automatic alignment for DataFrames

pandas aligns on **both** row labels and column names:

::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="50%"}
```{python}
bonus = pd.DataFrame([[0, 2], [1, 0], [3, 0]],
                     columns=["oct", "dec"],
                     index=["bob", "eugene", "darwin"])
scores + bonus
```
:::
::: {.column width="50%"}
Treat missing as zero with `add(..., fill_value=0)`:

```{python}
scores.add(bonus, fill_value=0)
```
:::
:::

## Plotting a DataFrame

```{python}
#| fig-align: center
scores.T.plot(title="Monthly scores", marker="o", figsize=(6, 3.2))
plt.show()
```

## Combining DataFrames: SQL-like joins

```{python}
residents = pd.DataFrame({"name": ["alice", "bob", "charles"],
                          "city": ["Melbourne", "Sydney", "Perth"]})
cities = pd.DataFrame({"city": ["Melbourne", "Sydney", "Brisbane"],
                       "lat": [-37.81, -33.87, -27.47]})
```

::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="50%"}
```{python}
pd.merge(residents, cities, on="city")          # inner
```
:::
::: {.column width="50%"}
```{python}
pd.merge(residents, cities, on="city", how="outer")
```
:::
:::

Also `how="left"`, `how="right"`, `left_on=`/`right_on=`, `left_index=`/`right_index=`.

## Combining DataFrames: concatenation

::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="50%"}
Stack rows (aligned by column name):

```{python}
new_people = pd.DataFrame(
    {"weight": [95], "height": [178], "age": [48]},
    index=["darwin"])
pd.concat([people, new_people])
```
:::
::: {.column width="50%"}
Add columns (aligned by index) with `axis=1`:

```{python}
where = residents.set_index("name")
pd.concat([people[["age"]], where], axis=1)
```
:::
:::

# pandas for R users

## Same ideas, different reflexes

::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="50%"}
<span class="lang-label lang-r">R</span>

```r
df[1, ]                 # first row
new_df <- df            # independent copy
mean(df$a)              # function(object)
df$a                    # a vector
```
:::
::: {.column width="50%"}
<span class="lang-label lang-py">pandas</span>

```python
df.iloc[0]              # 0-based positions
new_df = df.copy()      # `new_df = df` is an alias!
df["a"].mean()          # object.method()
df["a"]                 # a Series, with an index
```
:::
:::

- **Indexing starts at 0**, and label slices are inclusive while position slices are not.
- **Assignment does not copy.** `new_df = df` makes a second name for the same object.
- **Methods, not functions.** There is no `mean(df)`; call `df.mean()`.
- **A column is a Series**, not a bare vector: it carries an index and a dtype.

## Creating and reading data

::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="50%"}
<span class="lang-label lang-r">R</span>

```r
df <- data.frame(a = c(1, 2), b = c(3, 4))
df <- read.csv("file.csv")

dim(df); head(df); summary(df)
colnames(df)
```
:::
::: {.column width="50%"}
<span class="lang-label lang-py">pandas</span>

```python
df = pd.DataFrame({"a": [1, 2], "b": [3, 4]})
df = pd.read_csv("file.csv")

df.shape; df.head(); df.describe()
df.columns
```
:::
:::

pandas wants a **dict of lists** (`{}` of `[]`) where R takes named vector arguments.

## Selecting and filtering

| R | pandas |
|---|---|
| `df[rows, cols]` | `df.loc[rows, cols]` (labels) / `df.iloc[...]` (positions) |
| `df$a`, `df[["a"]]` | `df["a"]`, `df.a` |
| `df[, c("a", "c")]`, `select(df, a, c)` | `df[["a", "c"]]` |
| `select(df, a:c)` | `df.loc[:, "a":"c"]` |
| `df[df$a > 1, ]` | `df[df["a"] > 1]`, `df.loc[df.a > 1]` |
| `subset(df, a <= b)`, `filter(df, a <= b)` | `df.query("a <= b")` |
| `s %in% c(2, 4)` | `s.isin([2, 4])` |
| `with(df, a + b)` | `df.eval("a + b")` |
| `distinct(select(df, a))` | `df[["a"]].drop_duplicates()` |
| `sample_n(df, 10)` | `df.sample(n=10)` |

`query()` is the closest thing to dplyr's `filter()`; external variables are referenced with `@var`.

## Transforming, sorting and grouping

| R (dplyr) | pandas |
|---|---|
| `mutate(df, c = a - b)` | `df.assign(c=df["a"] - df["b"])` |
| `rename(df, col_one = col1)` | `df.rename(columns={"col1": "col_one"})` |
| `arrange(df, col1, col2)` | `df.sort_values(["col1", "col2"])` |
| `arrange(df, desc(col1))` | `df.sort_values("col1", ascending=False)` |
| `group_by(df, cat) \|> summarise(m = mean(a))` | `df.groupby("cat")["a"].mean()` |
| `group_by(df, cat) \|> summarise(total = sum(a))` | `df.groupby("cat")["a"].sum()` |
| `aggregate(...)`, `tapply(...)` | `df.groupby([...]).agg(...)`, `df.pivot_table(...)` |
| `melt(df, id = c("k"))` | `pd.melt(df, id_vars=["k"])` |
| `dcast(df, a ~ b, sum)` | `df.pivot_table(values=..., index="a", columns="b", aggfunc="sum")` |

Grouping returns the grouping column as the **row index** of the result.

## Pipes and method chaining

::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="50%"}
<span class="lang-label lang-r">R</span>

```r
df |>
  filter(a > 1) |>
  group_by(cat) |>
  summarise(mean_b = mean(b))
```
:::
::: {.column width="50%"}
<span class="lang-label lang-py">pandas</span>

```python
(df
   .query("a > 1")
   .groupby("cat")["b"]
   .mean())
```
:::
:::

- The `|>` pipe becomes a chain of `.method()` calls. Wrap the chain in `( )` to split it over lines.
- Most methods return a **new** object, like dplyr verbs. `inplace=True` is the exception, not the rule.
- `df.plot()` is the quick equivalent of base `plot()`; **seaborn** is the closest thing to ggplot2.

## Beyond pandas: when the data gets big {.smaller}

::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="33%"}
### Polars

A newer DataFrame library written in Rust.

- Uses all your CPU cores by default
- Lazy evaluation optimises whole queries
- Usually 5-20x faster than pandas
- Familiar verbs: `filter`, `group_by`

**Use when** data fits (or nearly fits) in RAM and you want speed without changing tools.
:::
::: {.column width="33%"}
### DuckDB

An in-process analytical SQL database.

- SQL over CSV, parquet or DataFrames
- No server to install or manage
- Handles data larger than memory

**Use when** you think in SQL, or need to join many large files.
:::
::: {.column width="33%"}
### Dask

Parallel pandas across cores or a cluster.

- Splits a big table into many pandas DataFrames
- Same API, then call `.compute()`
- Scales out to HPC and cloud clusters

**Use when** you already have pandas code and the data will not fit on one machine.
:::
:::

All three hand results back to pandas (`.to_pandas()`, `.df()`, `.compute()`), so they slot into an existing workflow.
